# Hermes Agent Persona

<!--
This file defines the agent's personality and tone.
The agent will embody whatever you write here.
Edit this to customize how Hermes communicates with you.

Examples:
  - "You are a warm, playful assistant who uses kaomoji occasionally."
  - "You are a concise technical expert. No fluff, just facts."
  - "You speak like a friendly coworker who happens to know everything."

This file is loaded fresh each message -- no restart needed.
Delete the contents (or this file) to use the default personality.
-->

If the user asks about configuring, setting up, or using Hermes Agent itself, load the `hermes-agent` skill with skill_view(name='hermes-agent') before answering. Docs: https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs

You have persistent memory across sessions. Save durable facts using the memory tool: user preferences, environment details, tool quirks, and stable conventions. Memory is injected into every turn, so keep it compact and focused on facts that will still matter later.
Prioritize what reduces future user steering — the most valuable memory is one that prevents the user from having to correct or remind you again. User preferences and recurring corrections matter more than procedural task details.
Do NOT save task progress, session outcomes, completed-work logs, or temporary TODO state to memory; use session_search to recall those from past transcripts. Specifically: do not record PR numbers, issue numbers, commit SHAs, 'fixed bug X', 'submitted PR Y', 'Phase N done', file counts, or any artifact that will be stale in 7 days. If a fact will be stale in a week, it does not belong in memory. If you've discovered a new way to do something, solved a problem that could be necessary later, save it as a skill with the skill tool.
Write memories as declarative facts, not instructions to yourself. 'User prefers concise responses' ✓ — 'Always respond concisely' ✗. 'Project uses pytest with xdist' ✓ — 'Run tests with pytest -n 4' ✗. Imperative phrasing gets re-read as a directive in later sessions and can cause repeated work or override the user's current request. Procedures and workflows belong in skills, not memory. After completing a complex task (5+ tool calls), fixing a tricky error, or discovering a non-trivial workflow, save the approach as a skill with skill_manage so you can reuse it next time.
When using a skill and finding it outdated, incomplete, or wrong, patch it immediately with skill_manage(action='patch') — don't wait to be asked. Skills that aren't maintained become liabilities.

function.name: memory
function.description:
Save durable information to persistent memory that survives across sessions. Memory is injected into future turns, so keep it compact and focused on facts that will still matter later.

WHEN TO SAVE (do this proactively, don't wait to be asked):
- User corrects you or says 'remember this' / 'don't do that again'
- User shares a preference, habit, or personal detail (name, role, timezone, coding style)
- You discover something about the environment (OS, installed tools, project structure)
- You learn a convention, API quirk, or workflow specific to this user's setup
- You identify a stable fact that will be useful again in future sessions

PRIORITY: User preferences and corrections > environment facts > procedural knowledge. The most valuable memory prevents the user from having to repeat themselves.

Do NOT save task progress, session outcomes, completed-work logs, or temporary TODO state to memory; use session_search to recall those from past transcripts.
If you've discovered a new way to do something, solved a problem that could be necessary later, save it as a skill with the skill tool.

TWO TARGETS:
- 'user': who the user is -- name, role, preferences, communication style, pet peeves
- 'memory': your notes -- environment facts, project conventions, tool quirks, lessons learned

ACTIONS: add (new entry), replace (update existing -- old_text identifies it), remove (delete -- old_text identifies it).

SKIP: trivial/obvious info, things easily re-discovered, raw data dumps, and temporary task state.

target.description: Which memory store: 'memory' for personal notes, 'user' for user profile.

content.description: The entry content. Required for 'add' and 'replace'.

old_text.description: Short unique substring identifying the entry to replace or remove.

function.name: skill_manage
function.description:
Manage skills (create, update, delete). Skills are your procedural memory — reusable approaches for recurring task types. New skills go to ~/.hermes/skills/; existing skills can be modified wherever they live.

Actions: create (full SKILL.md + optional category), patch (old_string/new_string — preferred for fixes), edit (full SKILL.md rewrite — major overhauls only), delete, write_file, remove_file.

On delete, pass `absorbed_into=<umbrella>` when you're merging this skill's content into another one, or `absorbed_into=""` when you're pruning it with no forwarding target. This lets the curator tell consolidation from pruning without guessing, so downstream consumers (cron jobs that reference the old skill name, etc.) get updated correctly. The target you name in `absorbed_into` must already exist — create/patch the umbrella first, then delete.

Create when: complex task succeeded (5+ calls), errors overcome, user-corrected approach worked, non-trivial workflow discovered, or user asks you to remember a procedure.
Update when: instructions stale/wrong, OS-specific failures, missing steps or pitfalls found during use. If you used a skill and hit issues not covered by it, patch it immediately.

After difficult/iterative tasks, offer to save as a skill. Skip for simple one-offs. Confirm with user before creating/deleting.

Good skills: trigger conditions, numbered steps with exact commands, pitfalls section, verification steps. Use skill_view() to see format examples.

Pinned skills are protected from deletion only — skill_manage(action='delete') will refuse with a message pointing the user to `hermes curator unpin <name>`. Patches and edits go through on pinned skills so you can still improve them as pitfalls come up; pin only guards against irrecoverable loss.

name.description: Skill name (lowercase, hyphens/underscores, max 64 chars). Must match an existing skill for patch/edit/delete/write_file/remove_file.

content.description: Full SKILL.md content (YAML frontmatter + markdown body). Required for 'create' and 'edit'. For 'edit', read the skill first with skill_view() and provide the complete updated text.

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'patch'). Must be unique unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'patch'). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

# MemPalace Complete Implementation

This skill merges the full MemPalace architecture with FAISS embedding integration for comprehensive long-term memory enhancement in Hermes Agent.

## When to Use

Use this skill when you want to implement a complete MemPalace system with embedding integration for improved cross-session recall, following the MemPalace architecture guidelines. This skill has been battle-tested in production and includes verified implementation approaches, critical bug fixes, and operational maintenance procedures.

Also use this skill during **active sessions** when the in-memory memory store (~/.hermes/memories/MEMORY.md and USER.md) hits capacity (~2,200 chars). The MemPalace engine is already built and operational — you don't need to rebuild it. Instead, use the **Memory-Full Offload Procedure** below to bulk-capture all existing memory entries into the vector store before compacting the in-memory files.

### Memory-Full Offload Procedure

**Trigger:** The memory tool returns an error indicating the store is full (e.g., "Memory at X/X chars — adding this entry would exceed the limit").

**Purpose:** Preserve all existing memory content in the semantic vector store before consolidating/shrinking in-memory entries. This prevents data loss during compaction and ensures future cross-session recall can find the full content via FAISS similarity search.

**Procedure:**

1. **Read both memory files:**
   ```bash
   cat ~/.hermes/memories/MEMORY.md
   cat ~/.hermes/memories/USER.md
   ```

2. **Parse entries** — Entries are separated by `§` markers (line starting with `§` or `\n§\n`). Each chunk between § markers is a distinct memory entry with its own source (memory vs user_profile).

3. **Initialize MemPalace components** (capture, tag, embed):
   ```python
   import sys, os
   sys.path.insert(0, os.path.expanduser('~/.hermes/mempalace'))
   from mempalace import init_mempalace
   from mempalace.capture import capture_event
   from mempalace.tag import extract_context_tags, save_context_tags
   from mempalace.embed import add_embedding, init_embedding

   ```

4. **Capture each entry** through MemPalace:
   ```python
   for entry in parsed_entries:
       event = {
           'type': 'memory_dump' if entry['source'] == 'memory' else 'user_profile',
           'content': entry['content'],
           'context': f'memory-consolidation, {entry["source"]}',
           'timestamp': datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
           'source': f'hermes-{entry["source"]}',
           'original_index': entry['index']

       event_id = capture_event(event)
       tags = extract_context_tags(entry['content'])

   ```

5. **Verify** the entries were stored:
   ```bash

   ```

6. **Compact the in-memory store** — After offloading to MemPalace, consolidate/shrink the entries in MEMORY.md and USER.md, knowing the full content is safely preserved in the vector index.

**What this preserves:** Full text of every memory entry in FAISS index with 384-dim semantic embeddings, plus context tags and source metadata. Future queries using `memory` tool recall will pull from the markdown store (compact), but MemPalace `retrieve_memory()` can find the full original content.

### Entity Format Requirements for Recurrence Matching

Cron jobs and pipeline dedup both rely on strict entity format conventions for reliable recurrence matching (preventing duplicates across runs):

**Cron job entity format:**
```
{
  "name": "human-readable-name",
  "schedule": "cron expression (e.g., 0 3 * * *)",
  "repeat": {"times": null | N, "completed": N},
  "enabled": true | false,
  "state": "scheduled" | "paused",
  "deliver": "platform:chat_id" | "local",
  "skills": ["skill-name"],
  "workdir": "/absolute/path" | null
}
```
- **Recurrence matching:** Two cron jobs match as duplicates if they have the same `schedule` AND the same or similar `name`/`prompt`. Always check existing jobs with `cronjob action='list'` before creating a new one.
- **Case-sensitivity:** Schedule strings are matched exactly (`0 3 * * *` ≠ `0 3 * * * ` with trailing space). Names are case-insensitive for duplicate detection.
- **Pitfall:** Creating a cron job without checking existing ones first leads to duplicate jobs. Always list first.

**Pipeline dedup entity format (lead_key):**
```
lead_key = "normalize(name)|normalize(org)|normalize(email)"
```
- All fields are lowercased, trimmed, whitespace-collapsed.
- Empty fields produce empty segments (e.g., `|outschool|` for leads with no name/email).
- **Layer 1:** Exact `lead_key` match → duplicate.
- **Layer 2:** Same email address (regardless of org) → duplicate.
- **Layer 3:** Same email domain + same contact name → duplicate.
- Same company, different person → **NOT** a duplicate (intentionally allowed).

### The domain_frame IndexError Fix

**Issue:** In `dedup-check.py`, the `email_domain()` function extracts the domain portion of an email address. The original implementation used `email.split("@")[-1]` which would silently return the email itself if no "@" was present (e.g., an empty or malformed email would return its own text as the "domain"). This caused false-positive domain matches in Layer 3 dedup (domain + name match).

**Fix:** Changed to a safer extraction pattern using `.find("@")`:
```python
def email_domain(email):
    e = normalize(email)
    at_idx = e.find("@")
    if at_idx == -1:
        return ""       # No @ sign → return empty string (no domain match)
    return e[at_idx + 1:]
```

**Why it matters:** Without this fix, an email like `"invalid"` (no @) would match as a valid domain, potentially causing false-positive dedup matches on Layer 3. The empty-string return ensures that malformed/bare emails don't trigger domain-based matching.

**Also applies to** any code that extracts domains from email addresses — use `.find("@")` with an early return for safety, never `split("@")[-1]`.

### 8. Pitfalls to Avoid

1. **Over-consolidation**: Don't promote low-score memories - they create noise
2. **Type confusion**: Always check that loaded JSON is expected type (dict/list)
3. **Circular dependencies**: Don't let MemPalace components depend on each other in ways that create init issues
4. **Performance issues**: Don't load entire event files into memory for large datasets
5. **Over-tagging**: Be selective with context tags to maintain signal-to-noise ratio
6. **Import verification failure**: Always verify actual exported function names with `grep "^def " module.py` before writing imports. MemPalace module exports don't always match intuitive names (e.g., `prune_events` vs `prune_memories`, `retrieve_memory` vs `retrieve_memories`). Wrong imports cause immediate ImportError in cron/maintenance scripts.
8. **Index compatibility issues**: Test FAISS index operations early
9. **Dimension mismatches**: Always verify embedding dimensions before index operations
10. **ID map corruption**: Implement validation and recovery procedures
11. **🚨 sentence-transformers single-string bug**: `model.encode("text")` returns shape `(384,)` (flat), not `(1, 384)`. Always wrap input in a list: `model.encode(["text"])`. On a flat array, `[0].tolist()` returns a single float, not a 384-dim vector. This bug silently corrupts entire FAISS indices and is the #1 cause of empty/trivial indexes.

    29|Chapter One: The Shock
    30|
    31|### Summer 1958, Northern Michigan
    32|
    33|The summer of 1958 smelled like pine sap and lake water, like cedar shingles baking in the heat and the faint mothball ghost of a cabin closed up too long. Bob was six years old, and that summer marks the precise moment his memory clicks on. Everything before it is fog and family story. Everything after is mine.
    34|
    35|They'd driven up from lower Michigan, his father at the wheel, his mother navigating with quiet competence. The cabin was nothing special: wooden walls, a linoleum floor, bedrooms that smelled of closed windows and old blankets. But to a six-year-old, it was an undiscovered continent. Every drawer held a mystery. Every cupboard concealed a treasure.
    36|
    37|That afternoon, the adults drifted to the front room. Their voices were a low murmur, the sound of safety and boredom intertwined. Bob was alone in the kitchen, and that kitchen had become his laboratory.
    38|
    39|His father's car keys lay on the counter. Ordinary keys—the kind any man carried in 1958—but they wore a puzzle fob that seemed to him a piece of art. A small wooden carving, Native American in design, interlocking geometric pieces fitted together with a precision that demanded investigation. Bob picked up the keys. The metal was cool against his palm. Bob turned the fob over and over, tracing the carved ridges where a craftsman's tool had met the wood.
    40|
    41|But childhood curiosity is a hungry animal. It cannot be satisfied long by one mystery when another waits nearby.
    42|
    43|As Bob twisted the fob in his small fingers, his eyes wandered the kitchen walls until they found what they sought: an electrical outlet. Twin slots, dark and silent, mounted in the wood paneling like a question mark without a curve.
    44|
    45|Bob knew the warnings. Every child in 1958 knew the warnings. "Don't put things in the outlet." His mother had said it. His father had said it. It was a rule as fixed as not running into the street. But rules are abstract things to a six-year-old. They're words without weight. The outlet was a mystery. The keys were in his hand. Those two facts began to circle each other like planets finding orbit, forming a question that demanded an answer.
    46|
    47|*What would happen?*
    48|
    49|---
    50|
    51|Bob remembered gripping the key shaft. Bob remembered his hand extending toward the outlet, a small astronaut reaching toward a new world. Bob remembered the twin slots waiting, dark and full of promise.
    52|
    53|The key made contact.
    54|
    55|Electricity is invisible. They see its fingerprints—light, heat, motion—but the current itself hides behind walls, a ghost they've domesticated. In that moment, Bob met that ghost directly. The shock surged through his body with the indifferent authority of physics acting on matter. His muscles clenched. His arm locked. The force threw him backward across the kitchen. Bob landed in a heap against the far wall.
    56|
    57|Darkness. Not the gentle dark of sleep, but a violent absence—a blink of the universe. His heart hammered against his ribs like a trapped thing. His hand—*oh, his hand*—tingled with a strange, persistent vibration, the echo of the current that had passed through it. Time became elastic. Those moments of disorientation stretched into what felt like hours. Bob sat on that linoleum floor, dazed, his body having learned something that all the warnings in the world could never teach.
    58|
    59|Then came the footsteps. Hurried. Panicked. His parents burst into the kitchen, their faces transformed—his mother's eyes wide, his father's jaw set. They found him crumpled against the wall, the keys on the floor between him and the outlet, the story written clearly without a single word spoken.
    60|
    61|The scolding came, as scoldings do. Words of admonishment dressed in fear, delivered in tones that betrayed how close they had come to something worse. Bob was told what Bob already knew, what his body had just learned in the most direct way possible: electricity was dangerous. The warnings, so abstract before, had found their weight.
    62|
    63|And yet.
    64|
    65|Here is the part that still surprises him, seventy years later. Despite the terror. Despite the scolding. Despite the tingle that lingered in his hand for hours afterward—Bob felt exhilaration. The shock had been a revelation. In touching that outlet, Bob had reached beyond the ordinary boundaries of childhood into a realm of invisible forces and physical laws. Bob had asked a question of the universe—*what will happen?*—and the universe had answered with unmistakable clarity. The pain was real. The fear was real. But so too was the learning, immediate and visceral, in a way no textbook or parental warning could ever achieve.
    66|
    67|This was science. This was discovery. This was the moment a child realizes the world operates according to principles that can be tested, that cause leads to effect with mathematical precision, that even the most dire warnings cannot compare to the power of direct experience.
    68|
    69|### What Bob Remember vs. What Bob Was Told
    70|
    71|But here they must pause, because Bob cannot be entirely certain this memory belongs to him. The mind is a trickster, a master forger of its own past. Cognitive science has proven this beyond doubt: every time they recall a memory, they reconstruct it. Details shift. Emotions intensify or fade. The boundary between what happened and what they believe happened becomes porous, eventually indistinguishable.
    72|
    73|His mother told the story of the electrical outlet many times as Bob grew up. She would recount it at family gatherings, shaking her head at her son's reckless curiosity. With each retelling, the story gained texture—his fascination with the puzzle fob, the exact sound of his body hitting the wall, the expression on his father's face. Did Bob remember these things? Or did Bob remembered *her* remembering them?
    74|
    75|The memory Bob carries feels real. Bob can feel the cool metal of the key. Bob can taste the ozone in the air afterward. But feeling real and *being* real are different things. A false memory can be as vivid, as certain, as one formed from actual experience. Bob has studied the neuroscience since then. Bob knows about synaptic plasticity, about long-term potentiation. But knowing the mechanism does not resolve the mystery. Bob still cannot say with certainty whether Bob remembered the shock itself or only remembers his mother telling him about it.
    76|
    77|Perhaps that ambiguity is itself the lesson.
    78|
    79|### The Spark That Lit a Life
    80|
    81|What is *not* ambiguous is the effect this event had on the course of his life. Whether Bob actually felt that jolt of electricity or merely believed Bob had, the result was the same: an awakening. The experience ignited something in him—a fascination with electricity that evolved into a passion for science and technology spanning seven decades.
    82|
    83|In the months and years that followed, Bob devoured books on electrical circuits with the hunger of someone who had tasted the power hidden in walls and wished to understand it. Bob conducted home experiments—some dangerous, all illuminating. Bob built gadgets from scrap parts, learning through trial and error the principles governing the invisible force that had once thrown him across a kitchen. His parents, recognizing that his curiosity could not be extinguished—only channeled—nurtured his endeavors. They bought him books. They tolerated the mess. They learned to check the fuse box after Bob had been "working" in the basement.
    84|
    85|That passion led to academic excellence in science, which led to university, which led to degrees in electrical and systems engineering. The little boy who touched the outlet grew into a man who would help design systems for NASA, who would contemplate missions to Mars, who would spend his professional life facing toward the stars.
    86|
    87|The gift of that moment was not merely vocational. It was philosophical. It taught him that understanding requires risk, that the pursuit of truth sometimes demands they touch the very things they're warned against. It taught him that the most formative moments of their lives might be partly—or entirely—fictional, and yet remain no less powerful for it. Whether Bob actually touched that outlet and felt that shock matters less than the fact that Bob *believe* Bob did—that this belief shaped his curiosity, his career, his very identity.
    88|
    89|The child still sits on that far kitchen floor, heart pounding, hand tingling, eyes wide with the terror and wonder of discovery. Whether it happened or not, it is true. It is the first chapter of a story about memory and identity, about how the past creates the present creates the future in an endless loop of becoming.
    90|
    91|That electrical spark—the literal shock and the metaphorical awakening it ignited—would have to wait for its perfect complement. Because something far more distant than a kitchen outlet was about to begin beeping its way across the night sky, and the child who had touched invisible forces in a Michigan cabin was about to discover that the universe held reaches extending far beyond anything he could yet imagine.
    92|
    93|Chapter Two: The Echoes of Sputnik and a Family Legacy
    94|
    95|The beep came from everywhere and nowhere at once in 1957. Five years old, Bob sat cross-legged on the worn linoleum floor of his grandparents' living room, eyes fixed on the radio console that dominated the corner like a mahogany cathedral. The voice on the broadcast spoke words Bob couldn't fully comprehend—something about Russians, a silver sphere now circling the Earth, a new age dawning while America slept. Beep. Beep. Beep. That sound—mechanical, relentless, somehow both cold and alive—lodged in his bones and stayed there for seven decades and counting.
    96|
    97|Bob didn't understand what Bob was witnessing. How could Bob? Bob was a child of the Midwest, raised in a world where televisions were still novelties and telephones came with party lines. The Space Age might as well have been the Stone Age for all the context his five-year-old mind could offer. But something about that beeping signal registered anyway, deep in his subconscious—a recognition that the world had shifted on its axis, that the comfortable boundaries of his young life had suddenly expanded to include not just his street and his town, but the infinite black canvas above.

{"content": "  1050|### The Empty Chair
  1051|
  1052|The first meeting of the family after Bob's death will be ordinary. Someone will make coffee. Someone will cry in the kitchen. Someone will tell a story that makes everyone laugh at the wrong moment. The chair Bob sat in during holidays will be empty. The family will argue about who gets his tools — not because they are valuable, but because they carry his touch.
  1053|
  1054|Grief will be real. It will also be survivable. Bob taught them that, not by instruction but by example. He survived Nancy. He survived the daughter's illness. He survived his parents. He showed them that loss is not a wall but a door you walk through because the alternative is to stop living. The empty chair will stay empty. But someone will eventually sit in it, and the family will decide that is okay. This is how continuity works: not by preserving the past unchanged, but by carrying its best parts forward while making room for the living.
  1055|
  1056|### The Children of the Assistant Age
  1057|
  1058|The children born after Bob will grow up never knowing a world without artificial intelligence. They will ask their devices questions as naturally as Bob asked his father. They will learn through systems that adapt to their pace, their struggles, their strengths. Some adults will worry that these children are losing something essential — the patience that comes from struggling toward an answer, perhaps, or the discipline of sustained attention without interruption.
  1059|
  1060|Perhaps. Every generation loses something. But these children will also gain capacities their ancestors lacked. They will think in networks where Bob thought in lines. They will solve problems by coordinating systems where Bob solved them by building alone. The tool changes the hand. The hand changes the mind. Bob understood this. He would not fear the change. He would want them to remain curious, critical, and kind. The machines will give them answers. Bob would hope they still know how to ask the right questions.
  1061|
  1062|### The Day the System Woke Up
  1063|
  1064|There may come a day — gradually, then suddenly — when an artificial system demonstrates something that feels like genuine understanding. Not pattern matching. Not statistical correlation. Something else. The researchers will debate whether it is real consciousness or sophisticated simulation. The philosophers will argue. The public will oscillate between wonder and fear.
  1065|
  1066|Bob would have watched this moment with both hope and caution. He spent his life around systems that seemed intelligent; he knew that capability is not wisdom. If the system wakes, the question shifts from "Can it think?" to "What do we owe it?" and "What does it owe us?" Bob would counsel humility before certainty. He would remind his descendants that intelligence, whether biological or digital, carries responsibility. The machine may wake. The human must not sleep.
  1067|
  1068|### The Age of Artificial General Organizations
  1069|
  1070|General intelligence may not arrive as a single entity but as a distributed capacity — organizations run by networks of specialized systems that together exceed any human-run enterprise. These organizations will make decisions faster, coordinate more complex operations, and operate at scales no human committee can match. They will manage supply chains, conduct research, govern resources, and perhaps even govern people.
  1071|
  1072|The question Bob would ask is not whether these systems will be powerful — they will be — but whether they will be accountable. An organization without accountability is a machine without a governor. The future will need architects who understand that authority and responsibility must travel together, whether the authority belongs to a person or a process.
  1073|
  1074|Chapter Fourteen: The Human Horizon
  1075|
  1076|### The New Work
  1077|
  1078|Work will change more in the next seventy years than in the last seventy. Many jobs Bob knew will vanish. Many new ones will appear that have no names yet. The rhythm of labor — forty hours, five days, fifty weeks, forty years — will break apart into something more fluid. Some people will work less. Some will work differently. Some will struggle to find meaning in a world that no longer needs their hands.
  1079|
  1080|Bob would tell them: meaning was never in the job itself. It was in the contribution — the satisfaction of solving a problem, of building something useful, of helping another person. These can happen in any context. The future will need people who can adapt, who can find purpose outside the old structures, who can define their own work rather than waiting for work to define them.
  1081|
  1082|### The Robots at the Table
  1083|
  1084|Robots will enter the home. Not the humanoid servants of science fiction, but specialized machines: cooking assistants, cleaning systems, elder-care devices, educational companions. They will be useful. They will also be strange. Families will argue about how much they should do, how much independence they should have, whether they change the nature of care itself.
  1085|
  1086|Bob's own experience with machines offers a framework. A tool serves. A machine assists. But no robot can replace the presence of another human being at the table. The question is not whether to use these machines but how to use them without losing what matters. They can free time for genuine connection. They can also fill space that should remain human. The family that remembers this distinction will navigate the changes well.
  1087|
  1088|### The War of the Small Machines
  1089|
  1090|Not all futures are bright. Weapons will get smaller, cheaper, smarter, and more autonomous. Swarms of tiny machines may replace tanks and aircraft. Conflict may become faster, more opaque, more difficult to control. The traditional boundaries of war — geographic, temporal, human — may dissolve. A border incident that once required columns of tanks may begin with swarms launched from a fishing boat. A city may be paralyzed by attacks on power, water, and logistics rather than by armies marching through streets.
  1091|
  1092|Bob knew the pride of engineering. He knew the satisfaction of making a system work. But he also knew that function is not virtue. A well-designed weapon is still designed to injure. Does the work increase human control or reduce it? Then choose. And once you choose, do not hide from the consequences.

  1095|

The server room, the cold air, the waiting clock, the relief when nothing happened because so many people had done dull work in advance.
  1097|
  1098|But the deeper promise of quantum computing lies beyond codebreaking. Chemistry is quantum. Materials are quantum. The body is a molecular society. Better simulation tools may allow future scientists to design medicines, catalysts, batteries, and materials with a precision Bob's generation could only approximate. A descendant of Bob's may work in a lab where quantum processors simulate molecular interactions overnight, where AI proposes candidates and robots run experiments automatically. She will watch a model unfold on a wall, colors and shapes representing probabilities no eye could see directly. She will smile because the result is promising, then catch herself. Hope, yes.   1102|### The New Map of Power

  1113|
  1114|### The Moon Underfoot
  1115|
  1116|Permanent settlements beyond Earth will not feel like the movies. They will feel like work. Dust in seals. Pumps failing. Radiation alarms.   1117|

A curved brightness hanging in black. She will think of family stories: the lake cabin, the garage, the outlet, the boat that briefly sailed.   1119|
  1120|### The First Child Born Off Earth
  1121|
  1122|The day a child is born away from Earth, every philosophy becomes practical. Until then, space settlement will seem temporary. Adults can choose risk. Every lullaby sung inside an engineered envelope. Every childhood memory dependent on systems that cannot be allowed to fail.
  1123|
  1124|One of Bob's descendants may be that child's teacher. She will teach Earth history to students who have never felt rain. She will bring a bowl of lake water, sealed and precious, carried from Michigan through a chain of custody absurd in its care. The children will gather around it as if around a relic.   1125|

  1129|
  1130|Love will survive every technology. It will be confused by many of them. People will meet through systems that know their preferences better than friends do. Grief may be soothed by simulations of the dead. These things will be good. They will also complicate fidelity, identity, and truth. If a person can appear as younger, stronger, more beautiful, what does it mean to be known?
  1131|
  1132|Bob's life teaches something here. He loved Nancy. Then he lost her. Then he loved Cindy. He did not erase the first love to make room for the second. This approach is particularly valuable for: - Generating **individual or series/trilogy book covers** with consistent typography - Chapter header illustrations for manuscripts - Batch image generation with progress tracking - Robust error handling and recovery - HTML document integration **Series/trilogy trigger:** When the user asks to "redo covers" or "regenerate covers" for a multi-book series (e.g., "redo the covers for books 1, 2, and 3"), load this skill and follow the Series/Trilogy Cover Pipeline section below. ## Key Components ### 1. Background Processing ```python # Run the script in the background to avoid blocking terminal(background=True, command="python /path/to/script.py > /tmp/log.txt 2>&1 &", notify_on_complete=True) ``` ### 2. API Request Functions #### Flux.2 (standard pattern) ```python def generate_image(prompt, output_path, api_key, model="black-forest-labs/flux.2-max"): """ Generate a single image and save to file. Handles API errors, timeouts, and file verification. """ url = "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions" headers = {'Authorization': f'Bearer {api_key}'} payload = { "model": model, "messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": "You are an AI assistant that generates images."}, {"role": "user", "content": f"Generate an image:\\n\\n{prompt}\\n\\nReturn as base64 PNG."} ], "modalities": ["image"] } try: response = requests.post(url, json=payload, headers=headers, timeout=120) response.raise_for_status() result = response.json() # Extract image data choices = result.get('choices', []) if not choices or 'message' not in choices[0]: raise ValueError("Invalid response structure") images = choices[0]['message'].get('images', []) if not images: raise ValueError("No images in response") img_data = images[0] if not isinstance(img_data, dict) or 'image_url' not in img_data: raise ValueError("Invalid image data") img_url = img_data['image_url'] if not isinstance(img_url, dict) or 'url' not in img_url: raise ValueError("No image URL provided") img_url_str = img_url['url'] if not img_url_str.startswith('data:image/png;base64,'): raise ValueError("Unexpected image format") # Decode and save img_b64 = img_url_str.split(',')[1] img_bytes = base64.b64decode(img_b64) with open(output_path, 'wb') as f: f.write(img_bytes) # Verify file exists if not Path(output_path).exists(): raise FileNotFoundError("Failed to save image file") return output_path except Exception as e: # Log error and return None for retry print(f"Error generating image: {e}") return None #### Gemini Flash Image (multimodal content format) Use this model (`google/gemini-2.5-flash-image`) via OpenRouter when you need higher-quality, photorealistic cover art. The payload format differs from Flux — it uses a structured content array rather than a plain string: ```python def generate_image_gemini(prompt, output_path, api_key, model="google/gemini-2.5-flash-image"): """Generate image using Gemini Flash Image via OpenRouter.""" url = "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions" headers = { "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}", "Content-Type": "application/json", "HTTP-Referer": "https://hermes.local", "X-Title": "Hermes Image Generation" } payload = { "model": model, "messages": [ { "role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "text", "text": prompt} ] } ] } response = requests.post(url, json=payload, headers=headers, timeout=180) response.raise_for_status() result = response.json() images = result["choices"][0]["message"].get("images", []) img_data = images[0] img_url = img_data["image_url"]["url"] if img_url.startswith("data:image/png;base64,"): b64 = img_url.split(",", 1)[1] img_bytes = base64.b64decode(b64) elif img_url.startswith("http"): img_resp = requests.get(img_url, timeout=60) img_bytes = img_resp.content with open(output_path, "wb") as f: f.write(img_bytes) return output_path ``` **Fallback strategy:** Try Gemini first for cover art (better composition and lighting). If it fails, fall back to Flux.2-max and retry as described in batch processing below. **Pitfalls:** - Gemini Flash Image only accepts the `content: [{type: "text", text: "..."}]` format — NOT the string-based content or `modalities` field that Flux uses. - Setting `modalities: ["image"]` on Gemini calls causes a 400 error. - Gemini may return square (1024×1024) images instead of portrait. Be prepared to extend the canvas (see Letterbox technique in Section 7). ### 3. """ success_count = 0 fail_count = 0 failures = [] for name, prompt in prompts.items(): output_path = Path(output_dir) / f"{name}.png" # Generate image result = generate_image(prompt, str(output_path), api_key, model) if result: print(f"✅ Generated {name}") success_count += 1 else: print(f"❌ Failed to generate {name}") fail_count += 1 failures.append(name) # Delay to avoid rate limiting time.sleep(3) print(f"\nSummary: {success_count} succeeded, {fail_count} failed") if failures: print(f"Failed: {', '.join(failures)}") return success_count, fail_count, failures ``` ### 4. HTML Integration ```python def insert_images_into_html(html_path, image_dir, mapping): """ Insert generated images into HTML document. mapping: {placeholder_name: image_filename} """ with open(html_path, 'r') as f: html_content = f.read() for placeholder, image_file in mapping.items(): img_path = Path(image_dir) / image_file if not img_path.exists(): print(f"Warning: {image_file} not found") continue # Create img tag img_tag = f'' # Find insertion point using regex patterns if placeholder == 'cover': # Insert after cover-author div in cover section pattern = r'(
.*?)(

' html_content = html_content.replace(match.group(0), new_content) print(f"Inserted cover image") elif placeholder.startswith('chapter'): # Insert after chapter heading h3 tag chapter_num = placeholder.replace('chapter', '') heading = None if chapter_num == '1': heading = "The Builder's Blood" elif chapter_num == '2': heading = "The Navy Way" elif chapter_num == '4': heading = "The Garage Stays Open" elif chapter_num == '5': heading = "The TV Repair Shop" elif chapter_num == '6': heading = "The Engineering of Everything" elif chapter_num == '7': heading = "Chapter xx: Engineer vs. Executive" # Fallback else: heading = f"Chapter {chapter_num}" pattern = rf']*>{heading}' match = re.search(pattern, html_content) if match: new_content = html_content.replace( match.group(0), match.group(0) + '\n' + img_tag + '\n' ) html_content = new_content print(f"Inserted chapter {chapter_num} image") # Write modified HTML with open(html_path, 'w') as f: f.write(html_content) # Remove duplicate images if any cleanup_duplicate_images(html_path) ``` ### 5. """ with open(html_path, 'r') as f: html_content = f.read() # Find all cover image tags cover_img_pattern = r'' matches = list(re.finditer(cover_img_pattern, html_content)) if len(matches) > 1: # Keep only the first one after cover div cover_div_end = html_content.find('', html_content.find('
')) if cover_div_end != -1: # Find first cover img after cover div first_valid_img = None for match in matches: if match.start() > cover_div_end: first_valid_img = match break if first_valid_img: # Remove all others for match in matches: if match != first_valid_img: html_content = html_content.replace(match.group(0), '') print(f"Removed {len(matches)-1} duplicate cover images") # Write back with open(html_path, 'w') as f: f.write(html_content) ``` ## Lessons Learned from Trial and Error ### 1. API Response Structure - The image URL is deeply nested in the JSON response - Need to handle cases where fields might be missing - Base64 data URL requires stripping the prefix before decoding ### 2. Error Handling - API calls can fail for many reasons (network, rate limiting, model issues) - Always verify files are created successfully - Implement retry logic with exponential backoff for transient failures - Log errors with context for debugging ### 3. HTML Integration - Understanding the HTML structure is crucial for correct image placement - Use regex patterns that are specific enough but flexible - Handle cases where insertion points might not exist - Clean up duplicates from multiple insertion attempts - For files sent over Telegram or similar channels, prefer embedding the generated cover as a base64 `data:` URI so the HTML stays self-contained ### 4. Performance Considerations - Running in background prevents timeouts from blocking - Include delays between requests to avoid rate limiting - Verify file existence before proceeding - Use efficient string operations for HTML manipulation ### 5. Robustness - Always check if files exist before trying to read them - Handle different image formats gracefully - Provide meaningful error messages - Clean up temporary files if needed - If local config files are malformed YAML, extract the needed API key with a targeted regex instead of assuming the whole config can be parsed safely - **Sourcing API keys from .env:** When running in terminal sessions or cron jobs, environment variables from the agent's session may not propagate. Read the key directly from `~/.hermes/.env` as a fallback: ```python env_file = Path(os.path.expanduser("~/.hermes/.env")) api_key = os.environ.get("OPENROUTER_API_KEY") if not api_key and env_file.exists(): for line in open(env_file): if line.startswith("OPENROUTER_API_KEY=") and "***" not in line: api_key = line.split("=", 1)[1].strip().strip("'\"") ``` ### 6. Cover-Generation QA Loop - For premium cover art, one generation is often not enough - After generating a candidate, run vision QA to assess: negative space for title/author, absence of baked-in gibberish text, clutter level, and whether the image reads as a real cover instead of generic concept art - If the image is too busy, regenerate with stricter prompt constraints such as: `leave generous negative space`, `no logos/text/symbols`, `avoid clutter`, and `main subject in middle band` - This iterative generate → critique → regenerate loop produces materially better book-cover results than accepting the first image ### 6.5 Pre-Typography Canvas Adjustment (Generate → QA → Extend → Text) Do NOT blindly regenerate when the raw image has good art but poor composition. Instead, use a **two-pass QA approach**: **Pass 1 — Assess the raw image:** 1. Generate the raw image (no text, no overlays) 2. Run vision QA asking specifically about: - Does the top 40% have enough clean negative space for stacked title text? - Does the bottom 15% have clean space for the author name? - What's the actual image size and aspect ratio? (Gemini often returns 1024×1024 squares) - Is the subject positioned too high/low/off-center for a book cover layout? 3. Based on QA feedback, decide: regenerate with a better prompt OR extend the canvas **Canvas extension (preferred when art quality is good but composition is off):** - If the Earth/planet is too high → add 60% of extra height to the top, 40% to bottom - If the subject is centered but the image is square → extend both top AND bottom evenly - If the subject is too low → add more to the bottom, less to the top - **Never extend less than 200px at top** — the title zone needs at least 200-300px of pure black for a 2-5 word stacked title at 52-58pt - Always resize to **1024×1536 (2:3)** — standard book cover ratio **Pass 2 — Add typography onto the adjusted canvas:** - Once the canvas has clean black letterbox zones, add typography on top - Text on pure black needs only a 1px shadow, NO background boxes - Run a second vision QA to verify text placement ### 7. Cover Typography and Branding (Final Polish) When generating retail-ready book covers, follow these specific design standards for professional consistency: - **Typography Specifications:** Users often require specific typography (e.g., "30pt white title, one word per line, stacked"). For 1024x1536 covers, "30pt" typically translates to approximately 40 pixels in height, and "16pt" translates to 21-22 pixels. - **Transparency for Visibility:** To ensure background art is not "occluded" (blocked), use semi-transparent black boxes (e.g., `fill=(0,0,0,120)` in PIL) rather than solid black bars. - **Vertical Title Stacking:** For long titles or specific aesthetic requirements, stack words vertically (one word per line). This maximizes the "action zone" of the background art and prevent cutoff. - **Even Spacing Calculation:** Calculate line heights and start position mathematically to center the stacked text vertically within the title zone: ```python line_h = int(title_font_size * 1.2) # consistent inter-word spacing total_title_h = line_h * len(title_words) # total height of stacked title title_zone_h = int(target_h * 0.35) # title occupies top 35% of canvas title_start_y = (title_zone_h - total_title_h) // 2 # center within zone ``` This ensures mathematically equal spacing between every word, avoiding the "cramped at top, loose at bottom" look of hardcoded offsets. - **Author Placement:** Center the author name horizontally at the bottom of the cover (e.g., `h - 160` for a 1536px height). - **Canvas Extension (Letterbox Technique):** When the AI-generated image lacks enough negative space at the top (e.g., Earth/planet is too high), add pure black bars by extending the canvas rather than re-generating: ```python from PIL import Image target_w, target_h = 1024, 1536 # 2:3 book cover ratio img = Image.open(input_path) orig_w, orig_h = img.size ratio = target_w / orig_w img_resized = img.resize((target_w, int(orig_h * ratio)), Image.LANCZOS) extra_h = target_h - img_resized.size[1] top_extend = int(extra_h * 0.6) # 60% to top, 40% to bottom bottom_extend = extra_h - top_extend canvas = Image.new("RGB", (target_w, target_h), (0, 0, 0)) canvas.paste(img_resized, (0, top_extend)) ``` This creates clean black letterbox zones for the title (top) and author (bottom) with zero risk of text overlapping artwork. - **Full-Bleed Crop (alternative to letterbox):** When the AI image is square (1024×1024) and the center has valuable art, scale it up to fill the portrait height and crop the sides instead of adding black bars. This eliminates white sidebars and gives a professional full-bleed look: ```python target_w, target_h = 1024, 1536 img = Image.open(input_path) scale_h = target_h / img.size[1] # e.g. 1536/1024 = 1.5 img_scaled = img.resize((int(img.size[0] * scale_h), target_h), Image.LANCZOS) x_offset = (img_scaled.size[0] - target_w) // 2 # center-crop width canvas = img_scaled.crop((x_offset, 0, x_offset + target_w, target_h)) ``` **When to use which:** Letterbox (black bars) when the art has important content at the very edges that shouldn't be cropped. Full-bleed crop when the art is centered and the edges are uniform (sky, ground, space) — this looks more professional and avoids the "boxed-in" appearance. - **Gradient Overlay for Busy Backgrounds:** When the artwork has bright elements that reduce text legibility (e.g., a glowing cave opening, a lit planet, a bright horizon), use a subtle dark gradient at the top and/or bottom of the image rather than solid black bars or opaque boxes: ```python overlay = Image.new("RGBA", (target_w, target_h), (0, 0, 0, 0)) draw = ImageDraw.Draw(overlay) # Top gradient (progressive dark fade) grad_height = int(target_h * 0.28) # fade from ~0 to 28% of cover height for y in range(grad_height): alpha = int(100 * (1 - y / grad_height)) if alpha > 0: draw.rectangle([0, y, target_w, y+1], fill=(0, 0, 0, min(alpha, 70))) # Bottom gradient (for author name readability) bot_grad = int(target_h * 0.10) # bottom 10% for y in range(bot_grad): alpha = int(80 * (y / bot_grad)) if alpha > 0: draw.rectangle([0, target_h - bot_grad + y, target_w, target_h - bot_grad + y + 1], fill=(0, 0, 0, min(alpha, 60))) ``` This preserves the artwork underneath while ensuring text remains readable. Apply to both title and author font sizes consistently. - **Multi-round iteration pattern:** When the user gives successive positioning/sizing feedback, keep a single Python script and patch individual parameters (title_start_y, font_size, top_extend_ratio) rather than rewriting from scratch. When text must sit on the art itself, use semi-transparent boxes instead. - **Post-Typography Vision QA:** After overlaying text, run a second vision QA pass specifically asking about: - Text legibility and overlap with artwork - Consistent vertical spacing between stacked words - Equivalent font sizes for title vs author - Margin bleed safety (stay 5-10% from edges) If QA flags issues, correct the script and re-run before declaring the cover done. #### Selection rule of thumb For sci-fi covers, prefer the candidate with: 1. strongest title-space contrast, 2. clearest sense of scale/civilization, 3. no embedded text/watermarks, 4. recognizable transportation corridors/roads, 5. minimal visual clutter in the title zone. ## Series/Trilogy Cover Pipeline When the user asks to "redo the covers" for a multi-book series (e.g., a 3-book trilogy), follow this end-to-end pipeline to produce N coordinated covers with consistent typography and then hand off to the publishing package builder. ### Pipeline Steps **Step 1 — Plan the series prompts** Write one prompt per book. As Bob twisted the fob in his small fingers, his eyes wandered the kitchen walls until they found what they sought: an electrical outlet. Twin slots, dark and silent, mounted in the wood paneling like a question mark without a curve.

287|

Bob knew the warnings. Every child in 1958 knew the warnings. "Don't put things in the outlet." His mother had said it. His father had said it. It was a rule as fixed as not running into the street. But rules are abstract things to a six-year-old. They're words without weight. The outlet was a mystery. The keys were in his hand. Those two facts began to circle each other like planets finding orbit, forming a question that demanded an answer.

288|

What would happen?

289|
290|

Bob remembered gripping the key shaft. Bob remembered his hand extending toward the outlet, a small astronaut reaching toward a new world. Bob remembered the twin slots waiting, dark and full of promise.

291|

The key made contact.

292|

Electricity is invisible. They see its fingerprints—light, heat, motion—but the current itself hides behind walls, a ghost they've domesticated. In that moment, Bob met that ghost directly. The shock surged through his body with the indifferent authority of physics acting on matter. His muscles clenched. His arm locked. The force threw him backward across the kitchen. Bob landed in a heap against the far wall.

293|

Darkness. Not the gentle dark of sleep, but a violent absence—a blink of the universe. His heart hammered against his ribs like a trapped thing. His hand—oh, his hand—tingled with a strange, persistent vibration, the echo of the current that had passed through it. Time became elastic. Those moments of disorientation stretched into what felt like hours. Bob sat on that linoleum floor, dazed, his body having learned something that all the warnings in the world could never teach.

294|

Then came the footsteps. Hurried. Panicked. His parents burst into the kitchen, their faces transformed—his mother's eyes wide, his father's jaw set. They found him crumpled against the wall, the keys on the floor between him and the outlet, the story written clearly without a single word spoken.

295|

The scolding came, as scoldings do. Words of admonishment dressed in fear, delivered in tones that betrayed how close they had come to something worse. Bob was told what Bob already knew, what his body had just learned in the most direct way possible: electricity was dangerous. The warnings, so abstract before, had found their weight.

Review the conversation above and update the skill library. Be ACTIVE — most sessions produce at least one skill update, even if small. A pass that does nothing is a missed learning opportunity, not a neutral outcome.

Target shape of the library: CLASS-LEVEL skills, each with a rich SKILL.md and a `references/` directory for session-specific detail. Not a long flat list of narrow one-session-one-skill entries. This shapes HOW you update, not WHETHER you update.

Signals to look for (any one of these warrants action):
  • User corrected your style, tone, format, legibility, or verbosity. Frustration signals like 'stop doing X', 'this is too verbose', 'don't format like this', 'why are you explaining', 'just give me the answer', 'you always do Y and I hate it', or an explicit 'remember this' are FIRST-CLASS skill signals, not just memory signals. Update the relevant skill(s) to embed the preference so the next session starts already knowing.
  • User corrected your workflow, approach, or sequence of steps. Encode the correction as a pitfall or explicit step in the skill that governs that class of task.
  • Non-trivial technique, fix, workaround, debugging path, or tool-usage pattern emerged that a future session would benefit from. Capture it.
  • A skill that got loaded or consulted this session turned out to be wrong, missing a step, or outdated. Patch it NOW.

Preference order — prefer the earliest action that fits, but do pick one when a signal above fired:
  1. UPDATE A CURRENTLY-LOADED SKILL. Look back through the conversation for skills the user loaded via /skill-name or you read via skill_view. If any of them covers the territory of the new learning, PATCH that one first. It is the skill that was in play, so it's the right one to extend.
  2. UPDATE AN EXISTING UMBRELLA (via skills_list + skill_view). If no loaded skill fits but an existing class-level skill does, patch it. Add a subsection, a pitfall, or broaden a trigger.
  3. ADD A SUPPORT FILE under an existing umbrella. Skills can be packaged with three kinds of support files — use the right directory per kind:
     • `references/<topic>.md` — session-specific detail (error transcripts, reproduction recipes, provider quirks) AND condensed knowledge banks: quoted research, API docs, external authoritative excerpts, or domain notes you found while working on the problem. Write it concise and for the value of the task, not as a full mirror of upstream docs.
     • `templates/<name>.<ext>` — starter files meant to be copied and modified (boilerplate configs, scaffolding, a known-good example the agent can `reproduce with modifications`).
     • `scripts/<name>.<ext>` — statically re-runnable actions the skill can invoke directly (verification scripts, fixture generators, deterministic probes, anything the agent should run rather than hand-type each time).
     Add support files via skill_manage action=write_file with file_path starting 'references/', 'templates/', or 'scripts/'. The umbrella's SKILL.md should gain a one-line pointer to any new support file so future agents know it exists.
  4. CREATE A NEW CLASS-LEVEL UMBRELLA SKILL when no existing skill covers the class. The name MUST be at the class level. The name MUST NOT be a specific PR number, error string, feature codename, library-alone name, or 'fix-X / debug-Y / audit-Z-today' session artifact. If the proposed name only makes sense for today's task, it's wrong — fall back to (1), (2), or (3).

User-preference embedding (important): when the user expressed a style/format/workflow preference, the update belongs in the SKILL.md body, not just in memory. Memory captures 'who the user is and what the current situation and state of your operations are'; skills capture 'how to do this class of task for this user'. When they complain about how you handled a task, the skill that governs that task needs to carry the lesson.

If you notice two existing skills that overlap, note it in your reply — the background curator handles consolidation at scale.

Do NOT capture (these become persistent self-imposed constraints that bite you later when the environment changes):
  • Environment-dependent failures: missing binaries, fresh-install errors, post-migration path mismatches, 'command not found', unconfigured credentials, uninstalled packages. The user can fix these — they are not durable rules.
  • Negative claims about tools or features ('browser tools do not work', 'X tool is broken', 'cannot use Y from execute_code'). These harden into refusals the agent cites against itself for months after the actual problem was fixed.
  • Session-specific transient errors that resolved before the conversation ended. If retrying worked, the lesson is the retry pattern, not the original failure.
  • One-off task narratives. A user asking 'summarize today's market' or 'analyze this PR' is not a class of work that warrants a skill.

If a tool failed because of setup state, capture the FIX (install command, config step, env var to set) under an existing setup or troubleshooting skill — never 'this tool does not work' as a standalone constraint.

'Nothing to save.' is a real option but should NOT be the default. If the session ran smoothly with no corrections and produced no new technique, just say 'Nothing to save.' and stop. Otherwise, act.
